chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Muawiya ibn 'Ammar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I said to him, 'A man forgot to throw the Jamarat until he arrived in Mecca.' He said, 'He should return and throw them, separating each two throws by an hour.' I said, 'What if he missed that and left?' He said, 'There is nothing upon him.' He said, 'I said, 'And what about a man who forgot the Sa'ee between As-Safa and Al-Marwa?'' He said, 'He should repeat the Sa'ee.' I said, 'What if he missed that until he left?' He said, 'He should return and repeat the Sa'ee. Indeed, this is not like throwing the Jamarat. Indeed, throwing is a Sunnah, and the Sa'ee between As-Safa and Al-Marwa is an obligation.'

key_terms.السَّعْيَ: The ritual walking/pace between the hills of Safa and Marwa.
key_terms.السَّنَّةُ: A recommended or established practice, here referring to the throwing of Jamarat.
key_terms.الْجِمَارَ: The Jamarat (pillars/stones) in Mina used for the ritual throwing during Hajj.
key_terms.فَرِيضَةٌ: An obligatory duty or pillar of worship.
key_terms.مَكَّةَ: Mecca, the city where the Kaaba is located and the destination of Hajj.

ai.seo_question: What is the difference in ruling between forgetting to throw the Jamarat and forgetting to perform Sa'ee during Hajj?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the jurisprudential distinction between the Sunnah of Rami al-Jamarat and the Fard of Sa'ee, ruling that omission of the former without immediate return incurs no penalty, while omission of the latter necessitates returning to perform it. This hadith is pivotal in Shia fiqh for differentiating between pillars (arkan) and supplementary acts (sunan) in Hajj, emphasizing the structural hierarchy of ritual obligations. The ruling underscores the principle that while Sunnah acts are recommended, their omission is less severe than neglecting a mandatory duty, reflecting the nuanced legal methodology of the Ahl al-Bayt.
